Abstract Objectives: On March 2020, the WHO declared coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. COVID-19 is associated with various clinical syndromes, with electrolytes imbalances involved. This review aims to quantify the prevalence and outcomes of hyponatremia among COVID-19 patients, as well as to review the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of hyponatremia among these patients. Methods: Using Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta Analyses guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature search using the electronic databases of Google Scholar, MEDLINE (PubMed), WHO Virtual Health Library, and ScienceDirect, without limitations regarding gender, geographical area, race or publication date, up until December 13, 2021. Primary outcomes measured were mortality, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, assisted ventilation need, and length of hospital stay (LOS). Secondary outcome was the mechanism underlying hyponatremia among COVID-19 patients. Results: From a total of 52 included studies, 23 underwent quantitative analysis. For the primary outcomes; proportions, odds ratios (OR), and standardized mean difference (SMD) were calculated using random effects model. The prevalence of hyponatremia was found to be 25.8%. Hyponatremia was found to be significantly associated with increased odds for mortality (OR = 1.97[95% CI, 1.50–2.59]), ICU admission (OR = 1.91 [95% CI, 1.56–2.35]), assisted ventilation need (OR = 2.04 [95% CI, 1.73–2.38]), and with increased LOS (SMD of 5.74 h [95% CI, 0.092–0.385]). Regarding the mechanisms underlying hyponatremia, syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) was most commonly reported, followed by adrenal insufficiency, and finally hypovolemic hyponatremia due to gastrointestinal losses. Conclusion: Hyponatremia among COVID-19 patients is generally associated with poor outcomes, with SIADH being the most common underlying mechanism. Hyponatremia is considered the most important and most common electrolyte disturbance that presents in clinical practice, with an increased risk of death.[10-12] The most prevalent cause of hyponatremia is the syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) contributing to nearly 50% of cases,[11] with an increase in this percentage in specific conditions such as brain and lung pathologies.[13] Several studies have demonstrated the prevalence of hyponatremia among COVID-19 patients.[14-16] However; in this review, we aimed to demonstrate the pooling prevalence of hyponatremia among patients with COVID-19 infection, with a focus on reflecting the impact of hyponatremia on the severity and outcome of the disease. fetched_contents.text: Cytokine Storm in COVID-19: Exploring IL-6 Signaling and Cytokine-Microbiome Interactions as Emerging Therapeutic Approaches Abstract IL-6 remains a key molecule of the cytokine storms characterizing COVID-19, exerting both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory effects. Emerging research underscores the significance of IL-6 trans-signaling over classical signaling pathways, which has shifted the focus of therapeutic strategies. Additionally, the synergistic action of TNF-α and IFN-γ has been found to induce inflammatory cell death through PANoptosis, further amplifying the severity of cytokine storms. Long COVID-19 patients, as well as those with cytokine storms triggered by other conditions, exhibit distinct laboratory profiles, indicating the need for targeted approaches to diagnosis and management. Growing evidence also highlights the gut microbiota’s crucial role in modulating the immune response during COVID-19 by affecting cytokine production, adding further complexity to the disease’s immunological landscape. Targeted intervention strategies should focus on specific cytokine cutoffs, though accurate cytokine quantification remains a clinical challenge. Current treatment strategies are increasingly focused on inhibiting IL-6 trans-signaling, which offers promise for more precise therapeutic approaches to manage hyperinflammatory responses in COVID-19. In light of recent discoveries, this review summarizes key research findings on cytokine storms, particularly their role in COVID-19 and other inflammatory conditions. It explores emerging therapeutic strategies targeting cytokines like IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ, while also addressing open questions, such as the need for better biomarkers to detect and manage cytokine storms. Additionally, the review highlights ongoing challenges in developing targeted treatments that mitigate hyperinflammation without compromising immune function, emphasizing the importance of continued research in this field. Keywords: IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ, cytokine storm, COVID-19, tocilizumab 1. Introduction This year marks four years since the COVID pandemic began, and although much has been documented, many unanswered questions remain about the intricate interplay of molecular pathways that occur with the dysregulation of the immune system. Although the uncontrolled release of cytokines is clearly detrimental to the organism, leading to multiorgan failure and high mortality rates, a clear separation between a normal and a dysregulated immune reaction in the case of a severe infection still demands continuous research. While cytokine storm (CS) characterizes the pathogeny of COVID-19, it is not specific to the SARS-CoV-2 infection, since this exaggerated immune reaction of the host organism has already been extensively linked to several diseases as a response to different pathogens, therapies, autoimmune disorders, and cancers [1]. In the 1990s, CS was first documented to be associated with graft-versus-host disease, and it was only later in the 2000s when the literature reported its critical role in infectious diseases caused by cytomegalovirus, influenza virus, Epstein–Barr virus-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, group A streptococcus, variola virus, or coronavirus. Interestingly, CS is also associated with non-infectious settings, notably called “macrophage activation system” in autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis [2]. Moreover, CS is also reported as a response to immunotherapeutic agents such as specific T cell-activating antibodies [3,4], while it is also induced by immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). The latter targeted therapy response is known in oncology as cytokine release syndrome, which encompasses CS and highlights the pluripotent role of cytokines in human pathophysiology [4]. Therefore, cytokines still present an important focus in research, since understanding their roles could elucidate important cellular and molecular mechanisms to improve diagnosis, prognosis, and better understand disease progression. Many factors contribute to the dysregulation of the host immune system in COVID-19, resulting in some patients being able to control the viral infection and develop asymptomatic, mild, or moderate forms, while others are unable to control the virus or limit the infection, leading to severe or critical forms, including ARDS with MODS or even death [1]. We have also previously shown that distinct profiles of cytokines and immune checkpoint molecules characterize disease severity and mortality in COVID-19 patients [5,6]. Thus, the scope of this review is to highlight recent advances in understanding CS in COVID-19 as an essential checkpoint guiding disease progression. The awareness by physicians tends to be low (5) although hyponatremia is associated with increased mortality and morbidity (6) such as gait instability (7, 8), falls (7), osteoporosis (9, 10), fractures (9, 10), and attention deficit (7, 8, 11). Each biomarker in non-ICU COVID-19 patients indicates a distinct but clinically meaningful signal: hyponatremia points to electrolyte disorder and poor prognosis, oxygenation index reflects respiratory compromise and severity, and IL-6 points to inflammation and cytokine storm risk.

Hyponatremia levels are associated with worse outcomes in non-ICU patients. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that hyponatremia was significantly associated with increased odds for mortality, ICU admission, assisted ventilation need, and increased length of hospital stay in COVID-19 patients [N1-F1]. The same review reported a pooled prevalence of 25.8% for hyponatremia, and it emphasized that hyponatremia on admission can be used to forecast length of hospital stay and severity of illness in COVID-19 patients [N1-F1]. Another review also described hyponatremia as a risk factor for adverse outcomes and as associated with demographic and clinical/laboratory parameters in COVID-19 patients [N1-R2]. While the evidence does not provide a single cutoff for “non-ICU” hyponatremia severity, it clearly supports that hyponatremia is a marker of worse outcomes in this population [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1].

Oxygenation index reflects respiratory compromise and disease severity. The evidence base here is indirect but consistent: oxygenation indices such as SpO2/FiO2 and PaO2/FiO2 are used to assess severity in hypoxemic patients and to predict mortality in COVID-19 [N2-R1][N2-R4]. A study noted that SpO2/FiO2 and ROX index at baseline significantly correlated with PaO2/FiO2 in a series of 100 moderate-severe COVID-19 patients [N2-R2]. Another source describes the oxygen saturation and fraction of inhaled oxygen as a noninvasive parameter that may independently predict 30-day mortality in COVID-19 patients [N2-R1]. Taken together, these findings suggest that lower oxygenation indices indicate more severe respiratory impairment and worse prognosis, even in non-ICU settings [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R4].

IL-6 levels suggest inflammation and potential cytokine storm risk. The evidence indicates that IL-6 is a central molecule in the cytokine storms characterizing COVID-19, exerting both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory effects [N3-F2]. A review also states that interleukin-6 levels ≥80 pg/mL predict an increased risk of severe disease progression in cytokine storm syndrome [N3-R2]. Additional evidence highlights that severely ill patients tend to have higher concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 compared to milder patients [N3-R5]. This means that elevated IL-6 levels are not just a sign of inflammation, but also a marker of cytokine storm risk and likely a therapeutic target in more severe disease [N3-F2][N3-R2][N3-R5].

Overall, the three biomarkers together point to a clinically actionable picture: hyponatremia is a marker of electrolyte imbalance and poor outcome, oxygenation index is a marker of respiratory compromise, and IL-6 is a marker of inflammation and cytokine storm risk [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2]. In non-ICU patients, these signals can help clinicians identify which patients are more likely to worsen, but they do not by themselves define a single treatment pathway [N1-R1][N2-R1][N3-R5].

Practical treatment guidance for non-ICU clinicians should be specific, evidence-informed, and cautious about combining these biomarkers into decision rules. The evidence supports separate management steps for each biomarker, but it also shows clear limitations in using them together as a single rule.

For hyponatremia, the supported management step is to recognize it as a risk marker and to avoid unnecessary fluid overload. The systematic review emphasized that hyponatremia on admission can forecast length of hospital stay and severity of illness in COVID-19 patients [N1-F1]. It also found that hyponatremia is associated with ICU admission, assisted ventilation need, and worse mortality [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a clear algorithm for fluid management in non-ICU patients, and it does not specify which sodium thresholds should be treated with restriction or correction. The safest inference is that clinicians should monitor sodium closely, avoid rapid correction unless there is clear evidence of severe hyponatremia, and consider underlying causes such as SIADH or adrenal insufficiency [N1-F1][N1-R5].

For oxygenation index, the supported management step is to use it as a guide for supplemental oxygen and respiratory support escalation. The evidence shows that SpO2/FiO2 and ROX index correlate with PaO2/FiO2 and may predict mortality in hypoxemic COVID-19 patients [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R4]. This supports using oxygenation indices to identify patients at risk of deterioration and to guide oxygen titration. However, the evidence does not provide a universally applicable oxygenation cutoff for non-ICU patients, and it does not specify whether a single index alone should trigger escalation. Clinicians should therefore use oxygenation indices in conjunction with clinical judgment, rather than as a standalone trigger [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R4].

For IL-6, the supported management step is to recognize it as a marker of cytokine storm risk and to consider anti-inflammatory treatment in more severe disease. The evidence states that IL-6 is a key molecule in cytokine storms and that tocilizumab is used to treat cytokine storm in severe COVID-19 [N3-F2][N3-R4]. It also notes that IL-6 levels ≥80 pg/mL predict increased risk of severe disease progression [N3-R2]. This suggests that IL-6 should inform treatment decisions when inflammation appears severe or when patients are approaching deterioration, but the evidence does not establish routine IL-6 monitoring or a specific cutoff for non-ICU patients [N3-F2][N3-R2][N3-R4]. A practical step is to use IL-6 in conjunction with other biomarkers and clinical signs, not as a stand-alone decision rule [N3-F2].

When to prioritize fluid management, oxygen support, or anti-inflammatory treatment depends on the dominant clinical signal. Hyponatremia points to fluid management and electrolyte vigilance, oxygenation index points to oxygen support and respiratory management, and IL-6 points to anti-inflammatory or anti-cytokine treatment [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2]. In patients with a combination of signals, clinicians should prioritize the most immediately threatening pathway. For example, if a patient has severe respiratory impairment plus elevated IL-6, the priority is oxygenation and anti-inflammatory treatment; if a patient has hyponatremia plus worsening oxygenation, the priority is fluid/electrolyte management and oxygen support [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2].

Limitations and gaps in the evidence are important. First, the evidence is not uniform across biomarkers. Hyponatremia evidence is strongest in hospitalized and ICU settings, but the question here is non-ICU patients, so the generalizability is uncertain [N1-F1][N1-R5]. Second, oxygenation index evidence is indirect and mostly derived from cross-sectional or cohort studies, not randomized trials, so it cannot fully guide treatment escalation [N2-R1][N2-R2]. Third, IL-6 evidence is promising but still limited by small sample sizes, lack of standardization, and the fact that cytokine storm is not the same as routine inflammation [N3-F2][N3-R2]. Fourth, the evidence for combining these biomarkers into a single decision rule is sparse. The strongest direct evidence linking IL-6 and sodium is in COVID-19, but the evidence does not provide a validated composite rule for non-ICU patients [N5-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3]. Fifth, the evidence is heterogeneous across studies, so clinicians should be cautious about over-interpreting correlations as direct treatment algorithms [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2].

In conclusion, the practical guidance is clear but cautious: monitor sodium closely, use oxygenation indices to guide supplemental oxygen and escalation, and use IL-6 as a marker of cytokine storm risk rather than as a single trigger for anti-inflammatory treatment [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2]. The main limitations are that the evidence is not sufficiently strong to support a single decision rule, that biomarker thresholds vary by study, and that cytokine and electrolyte signals may interact in ways not fully captured by the current literature [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2][N5-F3].

The strongest biomarker correlations appear in patients with severe respiratory disease, cytokine storm risk, and hyponatremia, while the evidence is weaker or more indirect in milder non-ICU patients.

The strongest biomarker correlations are seen in patients with more severe disease. The hyponatremia evidence repeatedly links low sodium to ICU admission, assisted ventilation need, and worse mortality in hospitalized and severe patients [N1-F1]. The IL-6 evidence links higher cytokine levels to cytokine storm, severe disease progression, and cytokine storm syndrome [N3-F2][N3-R2]. The oxygenation index evidence links lower oxygenation to worse outcomes and mortality in hypoxemic patients [N2-R1][N2-R4]. Together, these findings suggest that the strongest correlations occur in patients who are already approaching severe or critical disease, where hyponatremia, inflammation, and respiratory failure are more likely to coexist [N1-F1][N3-F2][N2-R1].

In terms of overlapping versus separate treatment needs, hyponatremia, oxygenation, and IL-6 suggest overlapping rather than completely separate priorities. The hyponatremia evidence points to electrolyte management and the need to avoid worsening fluid balance [N1-F1]. The oxygenation evidence points to respiratory support and oxygenation management [N2-R1][N2-R2]. The IL-6 evidence points to anti-inflammatory or anti-cytokine treatment [N3-F2][N3-R4]. These are not mutually exclusive: a patient can have all three signals simultaneously, and the treatment approach should address them together. For example, a patient with severe respiratory failure and elevated IL-6 may need oxygen support and anti-cytokine treatment, while also requiring careful fluid management to avoid precipitating hyponatremia or fluid overload [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2].

The strongest patient subgroups for biomarker correlation are those with respiratory compromise, cytokine storm, and hyponatremia. The evidence from COVIVA shows an inverse relationship between IL-6 and plasma sodium levels in COVID-19, with a stronger correlation in COVID-19 than in bacterial or other viral infections [N5-F3]. This suggests that patients with more intense inflammation, especially in COVID-19, are more likely to have overlapping hyponatremia and IL-6 elevations [N5-F3]. Similarly, the evidence that hyponatremia is associated with ICU admission, assisted ventilation need, and worse outcomes suggests that patients with severe respiratory disease are more likely to have poor electrolyte status [N1-F1]. Taken together, the strongest correlations occur in patients who are on the borderline between non-ICU and severe disease, where respiratory failure, inflammation, and electrolyte disturbance converge [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Treatment priorities should therefore be balanced rather than segmented. Hydration management is needed for hyponatremia, oxygen support for respiratory compromise, and anti-inflammatory or anti-cytokine treatment for elevated IL-6 and cytokine storm risk [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2]. The evidence also suggests that these priorities are not independent; for instance, inflammation may worsen respiratory function, and respiratory failure may worsen fluid balance [N5-F3][N3-F2].

A practical way to balance these approaches is to treat the most urgent signal first while monitoring the others. For example, a patient with severe hypoxemia may be prioritized for oxygen support, while IL-6 and hyponatremia are monitored and managed as secondary priorities. Conversely, a patient with a strong cytokine storm signal but stable oxygenation may be prioritized for anti-cytokine treatment. In patients with overlapping signals, the priority should be the most clinically threatening combination: severe respiratory failure plus cytokine storm plus hyponatremia is likely the subgroup where treatment decisions are most complex and where the evidence supports integrated rather than isolated interventions [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2][N5-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports shared treatment priorities in severe disease, but it also highlights divergent needs in less severe patients. The strongest correlations are in patients with respiratory compromise, cytokine storm, and hyponatremia, which means clinicians should integrate these biomarkers into a broader clinical picture rather than treat them as separate entities [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2][N5-F3].

**Hyponatremia** is strongly associated with worse outcomes in non-ICU COVID-19 patients. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that hyponatremia was significantly linked to increased odds of mortality, ICU admission, assisted ventilation need, and longer hospital stays [N1-F1]. This means hyponatremia is a marker of poor prognosis and should prompt closer monitoring and caution about fluid management.

**Oxygenation index** reflects respiratory compromise and disease severity. The evidence shows that oxygenation indices such as SpO2/FiO2 and PaO2/FiO2 are used to assess severity in hypoxemic patients and may predict mortality in COVID-19 [N2-R1][N2-R4]. **IL-6 levels** suggest inflammation and cytokine storm risk. The evidence indicates that IL-6 is a central molecule in the cytokine storms characterizing COVID-19 and that it exerts both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory effects [N3-F2]. A review also states that IL-6 levels ≥80 pg/mL predict an increased risk of severe disease progression in cytokine storm syndrome [N3-R2]. Additional evidence highlights that severely ill patients tend to have higher concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 compared to milder patients [N3-R5]. This means elevated IL-6 is not just a sign of inflammation, but also a marker of cytokine storm risk and likely a therapeutic target in more severe disease [N3-F2][N3-R2][N3-R5].

These biomarkers interact in a way that suggests **both shared and divergent treatment priorities**, depending on the patient subgroup. IL-6 points to anti-inflammatory or anti-cytokine treatment [N3-F2][N3-R4]. These are not mutually exclusive: a patient can have all three signals simultaneously, and the treatment approach should integrate them rather than treat them as separate entities [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2].

The strongest patient subgroups for biomarker correlation are those with respiratory compromise, cytokine storm, and hyponatremia.
